claim: Pain perception is decreased by shifting attentional focus away from a threatening event.
source: Pain perception is decreased by shifting attentional focus away from a threatening event.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational premise of the study.

claim: Attentional analgesia engages parallel descending control pathways from anterior cingulate (ACC) to locus coeruleus, and ACC to periaqueductal grey (PAG) – rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM).
source: This attentional analgesia engages parallel descending control pathways from anterior cingulate (ACC) to locus coeruleus, and ACC to periaqueductal grey (PAG) – rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM), indicating possible roles for noradrenergic or opioidergic neuromodulators.
evidence: This claim is supported by the study's findings and references to prior work.

claim: Noxious thermal forearm stimulation generated somatotopic-activation of dorsal horn (DH) whose activity correlated with pain report.
source: Noxious thermal forearm stimulation generated somatotopic-activation of dorsal horn (DH) whose activity correlated with pain report and mirrored attentional pain modulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI data presented in the study.

claim: Dorsal horn activity mirrored attentional pain modulation.
source: Noxious thermal forearm stimulation generated somatotopic-activation of dorsal horn (DH) whose activity correlated with pain report and mirrored attentional pain modulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI data presented in the study.

claim: Activity in an adjacent cluster reported the interaction between task and noxious stimulus.
source: Activity in an adjacent cluster reported the interaction between task and noxious stimulus.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI data presented in the study.

claim: ACC interacts with PAG and RVM to modulate spinal cord activity.
source: Effective connectivity analysis revealed that ACC interacts with PAG and RVM to modulate spinal cord activity.
evidence: This is based on effective connectivity analysis performed in the study.

claim: Blocking endogenous opioids with Naltrexone impairs attentional analgesia.
source: Blocking endogenous opioids with Naltrexone impairs attentional analgesia and disrupts RVM-spinal and ACC-PAG connectivity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the pharmacological manipulation in the study.

claim: Naltrexone disrupts RVM-spinal connectivity.
source: Blocking endogenous opioids with Naltrexone impairs attentional analgesia and disrupts RVM-spinal and ACC-PAG connectivity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the pharmacological manipulation in the study.

claim: Naltrexone disrupts ACC-PAG connectivity.
source: Blocking endogenous opioids with Naltrexone impairs attentional analgesia and disrupts RVM-spinal and ACC-PAG connectivity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the pharmacological manipulation in the study.

claim: Noradrenergic augmentation with Reboxetine did not alter attentional analgesia.
source: Noradrenergic augmentation with Reboxetine did not alter attentional analgesia.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the pharmacological manipulation in the study.

claim: Cognitive pain modulation involves opioidergic ACC-PAG-RVM descending control which suppresses spinal nociceptive activity.
source: Cognitive pain modulation involves opioidergic ACC-PAG-RVM descending control which suppresses spinal nociceptive activity.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Pain is a fundamental and evolutionarily conserved cognitive construct that is behaviourally prioritised by organisms to protect themselves from harm and facilitate survival.
source: Pain is a fundamental and evolutionarily conserved cognitive construct that is behaviourally prioritised by organisms to protect themselves from harm and facilitate survival.
evidence: This is a general statement about pain based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Pain perception is sensitive to the context within which potential harm occurs.
source: As such, pain perception is sensitive to the context within which potential harm occurs.
evidence: This is a general statement about pain based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: There are well-recognised top-down influences on pain that can either suppress or amplify its expression.
source: There are well-recognised top-down influences on pain that can either suppress (e.g. placebo Wager and Atlas, 2015 or task engagement Büssing et al., 2010) or amplify (e.g. catastrophising Gracely et al., 2004, hypervigilance Crombez et al., 2004 or nocebo Benedetti and Piedimonte, 2019) its expression.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Placebo can suppress pain expression.
source: There are well-recognised top-down influences on pain that can either suppress (e.g. placebo Wager and Atlas, 2015 or task engagement Büssing et al., 2010) or amplify (e.g. catastrophising Gracely et al., 2004, hypervigilance Crombez et al., 2004 or nocebo Benedetti and Piedimonte, 2019) its expression.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wager and Atlas, 2015.

claim: Task engagement can suppress pain expression.
source: There are well-recognised top-down influences on pain that can either suppress (e.g. placebo Wager and Atlas, 2015 or task engagement Büssing et al., 2010) or amplify (e.g. catastrophising Gracely et al., 2004, hypervigilance Crombez et al., 2004 or nocebo Benedetti and Piedimonte, 2019) its expression.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Büssing et al., 2010.

claim: Catastrophising can amplify pain expression.
source: There are well-recognised top-down influences on pain that can either suppress (e.g. placebo Wager and Atlas, 2015 or task engagement Büssing et al., 2010) or amplify (e.g. catastrophising Gracely et al., 2004, hypervigilance Crombez et al., 2004 or nocebo Benedetti and Piedimonte, 2019) its expression.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gracely et al., 2004.

claim: Hypervigilance can amplify pain expression.
source: There are well-recognised top-down influences on pain that can either suppress (e.g. placebo Wager and Atlas, 2015 or task engagement Büssing et al., 2010) or amplify (e.g. catastrophising Gracely et al., 2004, hypervigilance Crombez et al., 2004 or nocebo Benedetti and Piedimonte, 2019) its expression.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Crombez et al., 2004.

claim: Nocebo can amplify pain expression.
source: There are well-recognised top-down influences on pain that can either suppress (e.g. placebo Wager and Atlas, 2015 or task engagement Büssing et al., 2010) or amplify (e.g. catastrophising Gracely et al., 2004, hypervigilance Crombez et al., 2004 or nocebo Benedetti and Piedimonte, 2019) its expression.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Benedetti and Piedimonte, 2019.

claim: Top-down influences on pain influence both acute and chronic pain and provide a dynamic, moment-by-moment regulation of pain as an organism moves through their environment.
source: These processes influence both acute and chronic pain and provide a dynamic, moment-by-moment regulation of pain as an organism moves through their environment.
evidence: This is a general statement about pain modulation based on established knowledge.

claim: A simple shift in attention away from a noxious stimulus can cause a decrease in pain perception – a phenomenon known as attentional analgesia.
source: A simple shift in attention away from a noxious stimulus can cause a decrease in pain perception – a phenomenon known as attentional analgesia.
evidence: This is a definition of attentional analgesia based on established knowledge.

claim: Attentional analgesia can be considered to be a mechanism to enable focus, allowing prioritisation of task performance over pain interruption.
source: This effect can be considered to be a mechanism to enable focus, allowing prioritisation of task performance over pain interruption (Eccleston and Crombez, 1999; Erpelding and Davis, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Eccleston and Crombez, 1999 and Erpelding and Davis, 2013.

claim: Attentional analgesia is reliably demonstrable in a laboratory setting.
source: This phenomenon is reliably demonstrable in a laboratory setting (Miron et al., 1989) and a network of cortical and brainstem structures have been implicated in attentional analgesia (Bantick et al., 2002; Brooks et al., 2017; Bushnell et al., 2013; Lorenz et al., 2003; Petrovic et al., 2002; Peyron et al., 2000; Sprenger et al., 2012; Tracey et al., 2002; Valet et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Miron et al., 1989.

claim: A network of cortical and brainstem structures have been implicated in attentional analgesia.
source: This phenomenon is reliably demonstrable in a laboratory setting (Miron et al., 1989) and a network of cortical and brainstem structures have been implicated in attentional analgesia (Bantick et al., 2002; Brooks et al., 2017; Bushnell et al., 2013; Lorenz et al., 2003; Petrovic et al., 2002; Peyron et al., 2000; Sprenger et al., 2012; Tracey et al., 2002; Valet et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Two parallel pathways are implicated in driving brainstem activity related to attentional analgesia.
source: We have shown that two parallel pathways are implicated in driving brainstem activity related to attentional analgesia (Brooks et al., 2017; Oliva et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brooks et al., 2017 and Oliva et al., 2021b.

claim: Projections from rostral anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) drive the periaqueductal grey (PAG) and rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM), which animal studies have shown to work in concert using opioidergic mechanisms to regulate spinal nociception.
source: Projections from rostral anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) were found to drive the periaqueductal grey (PAG) and rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM), which animal studies have shown to work in concert using opioidergic mechanisms to regulate spinal nociception (Fields, 2004; Fields and Basbaum, 1978; Heinricher et al., 1994; Ossipov et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to animal studies.

claim: A bidirectional connection between ACC and locus coeruleus (LC) was directly involved in attentional analgesia.
source: Similarly, a bidirectional connection between ACC and locus coeruleus (LC) was also directly involved in attentional analgesia.
evidence: This is based on prior findings from the authors' research.

claim: The locus coeruleus is the primary source of cortical noradrenaline.
source: As the primary source of cortical noradrenaline, the LC is thought to signal salience of incoming sensory information (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Sara and Bouret, 2012), but can also independently modulate spinal nociception (De Felice et al., 2011; Hirschberg et al., 2017; Hughes et al., 2015; Llorca-Torralba et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the LC.

claim: The LC is thought to signal salience of incoming sensory information.
source: As the primary source of cortical noradrenaline, the LC is thought to signal salience of incoming sensory information (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Sara and Bouret, 2012), but can also independently modulate spinal nociception (De Felice et al., 2011; Hirschberg et al., 2017; Hughes et al., 2015; Llorca-Torralba et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005 and Sara and Bouret, 2012.

claim: The LC can independently modulate spinal nociception.
source: As the primary source of cortical noradrenaline, the LC is thought to signal salience of incoming sensory information (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Sara and Bouret, 2012), but can also independently modulate spinal nociception (De Felice et al., 2011; Hirschberg et al., 2017; Hughes et al., 2015; Llorca-Torralba et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The network interactions between brain, brainstem, and spinal cord and the neurotransmitter systems involved in producing attentional analgesia have yet to be elucidated in humans.
source: Although these animal studies provide a framework for our understanding of descending control mechanisms that are likely to be mediating attentional analgesia, the network interactions between brain, brainstem, and spinal cord and the neurotransmitter systems involved in producing attentional analgesia have yet to be elucidated in humans.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: The distributed extent of the network spanning the entire neuraxis from forebrain to spinal cord has only relatively recently become accessible using simultaneous imaging approaches in humans.
source: In part, this gap in our knowledge is because of the distributed extent of the network spanning the entire neuraxis from forebrain to spinal cord, which has only relatively recently become accessible using simultaneous imaging approaches in humans (Cohen-Adad et al., 2010; Finsterbusch et al., 2013; Islam et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent methodological advances.

claim: A total of 39 subjects completed the three fMRI imaging sessions.
source: A total of 39 subjects (mean age 23.7, range [18 - 45] years, 18 females) completed the three fMRI imaging sessions with a 2 × 2 factorial experimental design (RSVP task difficulty: easy or hard, thermal stimulus intensity: low or high, Figure 1).
evidence: This is a description of the study sample.

claim: The mean age of subjects was 23.7 years with a range of 18-45 years.
source: A total of 39 subjects (mean age 23.7, range [18 - 45] years, 18 females) completed the three fMRI imaging sessions with a 2 × 2 factorial experimental design (RSVP task difficulty: easy or hard, thermal stimulus intensity: low or high, Figure 1).
evidence: This is a description of the study sample.

claim: 18 of the 39 subjects were female.
source: A total of 39 subjects (mean age 23.7, range [18 - 45] years, 18 females) completed the three fMRI imaging sessions with a 2 × 2 factorial experimental design (RSVP task difficulty: easy or hard, thermal stimulus intensity: low or high, Figure 1).
evidence: This is a description of the study sample.

claim: The study used a 2 × 2 factorial experimental design with RSVP task difficulty (easy or hard) and thermal stimulus intensity (low or high).
source: A total of 39 subjects (mean age 23.7, range [18 - 45] years, 18 females) completed the three fMRI imaging sessions with a 2 × 2 factorial experimental design (RSVP task difficulty: easy or hard, thermal stimulus intensity: low or high, Figure 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: A different drug was administered orally before each scan session (naltrexone [50 mg], reboxetine [4 mg], or placebo).
source: A different drug was administered orally before each scan session (naltrexone [50 mg], reboxetine [4 mg], or placebo), which included whole CNS imaging with slice-specific z-shimming (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental protocol.

claim: The study included whole CNS imaging with slice-specific z-shimming.
source: A different drug was administered orally before each scan session (naltrexone [50 mg], reboxetine [4 mg], or placebo), which included whole CNS imaging with slice-specific z-shimming (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a description of the imaging methodology.

claim: The behavioural signature of attentional analgesia is a task*temperature interaction, driven by a reduction in pain ratings during the high temperature-hard task condition.
source: The behavioural signature of attentional analgesia is a task*temperature interaction, driven by a reduction in pain ratings during the high temperature-hard task condition (Brooks et al., 2017; Oliva et al., 2021a; Oliva et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A first level analysis of the pooled pain behavioural data across all experimental sessions showed a main effect of temperature (F (1,38) = 221, p = 0.0001).
source: A first level analysis of the pooled pain behavioural data across all experimental sessions showed: a main effect of temperature (F (1,38) = 221, p = 0.0001, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) with higher scores under the high temperature conditions; a main effect of task (F (1,38) = 4.9, p = 0.03); and importantly demonstrated the expected task*temperature interaction consistent with attentional pain modulation (F (1, 38) = 10.5, p = 0.0025, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: Higher pain scores were observed under the high temperature conditions.
source: A first level analysis of the pooled pain behavioural data across all experimental sessions showed: a main effect of temperature (F (1,38) = 221, p = 0.0001, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) with higher scores under the high temperature conditions; a main effect of task (F (1,38) = 4.9, p = 0.03); and importantly demonstrated the expected task*temperature interaction consistent with attentional pain modulation (F (1, 38) = 10.5, p = 0.0025, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: A first level analysis of the pooled pain behavioural data across all experimental sessions showed a main effect of task (F (1,38) = 4.9, p = 0.03).
source: A first level analysis of the pooled pain behavioural data across all experimental sessions showed: a main effect of temperature (F (1,38) = 221, p = 0.0001, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) with higher scores under the high temperature conditions; a main effect of task (F (1,38) = 4.9, p = 0.03); and importantly demonstrated the expected task*temperature interaction consistent with attentional pain modulation (F (1, 38) = 10.5, p = 0.0025, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: A first level analysis of the pooled pain behavioural data demonstrated the expected task*temperature interaction consistent with attentional pain modulation (F (1, 38) = 10.5, p = 0.0025).
source: A first level analysis of the pooled pain behavioural data across all experimental sessions showed: a main effect of temperature (F (1,38) = 221, p = 0.0001, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) with higher scores under the high temperature conditions; a main effect of task (F (1,38) = 4.9, p = 0.03); and importantly demonstrated the expected task*temperature interaction consistent with attentional pain modulation (F (1, 38) = 10.5, p = 0.0025, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: Subjects given Reboxetine showed a task*temperature interaction (F (1, 38) = 9.023, p = 0.0047).
source: Similarly, subjects given Reboxetine showed a task*temperature interaction (F (1, 38) = 9.023, p = 0.0047), again driven by decreased pain scores in the hard|high vs easy|high condition (31.9 ± 15.8 vs 35.6 ± 15.5, p = 0.0034, Dz = −0.42).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: In the Reboxetine condition, the task*temperature interaction was driven by decreased pain scores in the hard|high vs easy|high condition (31.9 ± 15.8 vs 35.6 ± 15.5, p = 0.0034, Dz = −0.42).
source: Similarly, subjects given Reboxetine showed a task*temperature interaction (F (1, 38) = 9.023, p = 0.0047), again driven by decreased pain scores in the hard|high vs easy|high condition (31.9 ± 15.8 vs 35.6 ± 15.5, p = 0.0034, Dz = −0.42).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: Naltrexone blocked the analgesic effect of attention with no task*temperature interaction (F (1, 38) = 0.4355, p = 0.5133).
source: In contrast, Naltrexone blocked the analgesic effect of attention with no task*temperature interaction (F (1, 38) = 0.4355, p = 0.5133), hard|high (37.4 ± 17.1) vs easy|high (38.3 ± 17.1), Dz = −0.11).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: Subjects in both the placebo and reboxetine conditions showed a significant decrease in pain score during the hard task that was not evident in the presence of naltrexone.
source: Further analysis of the attentional modulation of pain showed that subjects in both the placebo and reboxetine conditions showed a significant decrease in pain score during the hard task that was not evident in the presence of naltrexone (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, one sample t-test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: The plausible magnitude of the attentional analgesic effect under naltrexone was smaller than a 6% (< 2.3 point) reduction in pain score (p = 0.049).
source: We used equivalence analysis (TOST method described by Lakens, 2017) to demonstrate that the plausible magnitude of the attentional analgesic effect under naltrexone was smaller than a 6% ( < 2.3 point) reduction in pain score (p = 0.049) confirming it as being smaller than that seen in the presence of placebo or reboxetine.
evidence: This is a statistical result from equivalence testing.

claim: The effect of naltrexone was specific to attentional analgesia as naltrexone had no effect on the calibrated temperature for the high thermal stimulus or the speed of character presentation for the RSVP task.
source: This effect was specific to attentional analgesia as naltrexone had no effect on the calibrated temperature for the high thermal stimulus or the speed of character presentation for the RSVP task (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: The attentional analgesic effect is robust and reproducible between and across subjects.
source: Behaviourally these findings indicate that the attentional analgesic effect is robust, reproducible between and across subjects and that it involves an opioidergic mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral findings.

claim: The attentional analgesic effect involves an opioidergic mechanism.
source: Behaviourally these findings indicate that the attentional analgesic effect is robust, reproducible between and across subjects and that it involves an opioidergic mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral findings.

claim: Cervical spine fMRI revealed two distinct clusters of activity within the left side of the C6 cord segment.
source: Cervical spine fMRI revealed two distinct clusters of activity within the left side of the C6 cord segment. The first showing the main effect of temperature (red-yellow, Spinalnoci) and a second showing task*temperature interaction (blue-light blue, Spinalint) (significance reported with p < 0.05 (TFCE) within a left sided C5/C6 anatomical mask).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the spinal fMRI data.

claim: The first spinal cluster showed the main effect of temperature (Spinalnoci).
source: Cervical spine fMRI revealed two distinct clusters of activity within the left side of the C6 cord segment. The first showing the main effect of temperature (red-yellow, Spinalnoci) and a second showing task*temperature interaction (blue-light blue, Spinalint) (significance reported with p < 0.05 (TFCE) within a left sided C5/C6 anatomical mask).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the spinal fMRI data.

claim: The second spinal cluster showed task*temperature interaction (Spinalint).
source: Cervical spine fMRI revealed two distinct clusters of activity within the left side of the C6 cord segment. The first showing the main effect of temperature (red-yellow, Spinalnoci) and a second showing task*temperature interaction (blue-light blue, Spinalint) (significance reported with p < 0.05 (TFCE) within a left sided C5/C6 anatomical mask).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the spinal fMRI data.

claim: No cluster reached significance for the main effect of task in the spinal cord.
source: No cluster reached significance for the main effect of task.
evidence: This is a negative finding from the spinal fMRI data.

claim: Parameter estimates from the Spinalnoci cluster showed a positive correlation with the pain scores across all conditions.
source: Parameter estimates from the Spinalnoci cluster showed a positive correlation with the pain scores across all conditions (Pearson's Correlation, 95% CI).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the spinal fMRI data analysis.

claim: Parameter estimates from the Spinalnoci cluster revealed a decrease in BOLD in the hard|high versus easy|high condition, seen in placebo and reboxetine arms but not in naltrexone.
source: Parameter estimates from the Spinalnoci cluster revealed a decrease in BOLD in the hard|high versus easy|high condition, seen in placebo and reboxetine arms but not in naltrexone.
evidence: This is a result from the spinal fMRI data analysis.

claim: Extraction of parameter estimates from the Spinalint cluster revealed an increase in BOLD in the hard|high condition, across all three drug sessions compared to the easy|high and hard|low conditions (Friedman test p < 0.0001).
source: Extraction of parameter estimates from the Spinalint cluster revealed an increase in BOLD in the hard|high condition, across all three drug sessions compared to the easy|high and hard|low conditions (Friedman test p < 0.0001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the spinal fMRI data analysis.

claim: Following registration to the PAM50 spinal cord template, a cluster of activation representing the positive main effect of temperature was identified in the left dorsal horn (DH), in the C6 spinal segment.
source: Following registration to the PAM50 spinal cord template (see Figure 2—video 1), a cluster of activation representing the positive main effect of temperature was identified in the left dorsal horn (DH), in the C6 spinal segment (Figure 2B, assessed using permutation testing with a left C5/C6 mask, p < 0.05, TFCE corrected).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the spinal fMRI data analysis.

claim: The Spinalnoci cluster represents activity in a population of spinal neurons that responded more strongly to noxious thermal stimulation.
source: This represents activity in a population of spinal neurons that responded more strongly to noxious thermal stimulation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI findings.

claim: The Spinalnoci cluster was somatotopically localised, given that the thermal stimuli were applied to the left forearm in the C6 dermatome.
source: This Spinalnoci cluster was somatotopically localised, given that the thermal stimuli were applied to the left forearm in the C6 dermatome (and its location was also confirmed without masking, Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI findings based on anatomical knowledge.

claim: There was a positive correlation between the pain ratings and activity in the Spinalnoci cluster across all subjects and experimental conditions.
source: There was a positive corelation between the pain ratings and activity in the Spinalnoci cluster across all subjects and experimental conditions (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: In the placebo session, the pattern of BOLD signal change across conditions in the Spinalnoci cluster was similar to the pain scores.
source: Accordingly in the placebo session, the pattern of BOLD signal change across conditions was similar to the pain scores (Figure 2A and D), and the response to a noxious stimulus was lower in the hard|high than easy|high condition, suggesting that the Spinalnoci activity was modulated during attentional analgesia.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: The response to a noxious stimulus in the Spinalnoci cluster was lower in the hard|high than easy|high condition, suggesting that the Spinalnoci activity was modulated during attentional analgesia.
source: Accordingly in the placebo session, the pattern of BOLD signal change across conditions was similar to the pain scores (Figure 2A and D), and the response to a noxious stimulus was lower in the hard|high than easy|high condition, suggesting that the Spinalnoci activity was modulated during attentional analgesia.
evidence: This is an inference from the data analysis.

claim: A similar pattern of Spinalnoci activity was evident in the reboxetine condition.
source: A similar pattern was evident in the reboxetine condition however, this was not observed in the naltrexone arm consistent with the opioid antagonist-mediated blockade of attentional analgesia.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: The pattern of Spinalnoci activity was not observed in the naltrexone arm consistent with the opioid antagonist-mediated blockade of attentional analgesia.
source: A similar pattern was evident in the reboxetine condition however, this was not observed in the naltrexone arm consistent with the opioid antagonist-mediated blockade of attentional analgesia.
evidence: This is an observation and interpretation from the data analysis.

claim: The Spinalint cluster was located on the left side of the C6 segment but was slightly caudal, deeper and closer to the midline with respect to the Spinalnoci cluster (with only marginal overlap).
source: Analysis of the task*temperature interaction revealed a second discrete spinal cluster (Spinalint, Figure 2B). This was also located on the left side of the C6 segment but was slightly caudal, deeper and closer to the midline with respect to the Spinalnoci cluster (with only marginal overlap).
evidence: This is a description of the anatomical location of the cluster.

claim: The location of the Spinalint cluster was confirmed in an unmasked spinal analysis.
source: The location of this activity was again confirmed in an unmasked spinal analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a methodological confirmation of the finding.

claim: Extraction of BOLD parameter estimates from the Spinalint cluster in the placebo and reboxetine condition showed an increased level of activity in the hard|high condition compared to the easy|high and hard|low conditions.
source: Extraction of BOLD parameter estimates from the Spinalint cluster in the placebo and reboxetine condition, showed an increased level of activity in the hard|high condition compared to the easy|high and hard|low conditions (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis.

claim: The Spinalint cluster showed significant activation in the hard|high condition in the placebo and reboxetine trials which was not evident in the presence of naltrexone.
source: The Spinalint cluster showed significant activation in the hard|high condition in the placebo and reboxetine trials which was not evident in the presence of naltrexone (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis.

claim: The Spinalint cluster activity profile suggests this cluster, potentially composed of spinal interneurons, plays a role in the modulation of nociception during the attentional analgesic effect.
source: This activity profile suggests this Spinalint cluster, potentially composed of spinal interneurons, plays a role in the modulation of nociception during the attentional analgesic effect.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Analysis of the main effect of temperature within a whole brainstem mask showed substantial clusters of activity in the midbrain (PAG) and medulla (RVM) with more discrete clusters in the dorsal pons bilaterally (LC).
source: Analysis of the main effect of temperature within a whole brainstem mask showed substantial clusters of activity in the midbrain (PAG) and medulla (RVM) with more discrete clusters in the dorsal pons bilaterally (LC) (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the brainstem fMRI data.

claim: In the main effect of task, the pattern of brainstem activation was more diffuse but again included activation of the PAG, RVM, and bilateral LC.
source: In the main effect of task, the pattern of brainstem activation was more diffuse (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), but again included activation of the PAG, RVM, and bilateral LC.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the brainstem fMRI data.

claim: No task*temperature interaction was observed within the brainstem.
source: Importantly for the mediation of attentional analgesia, no task*temperature interaction was observed within the brainstem (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a negative finding from the brainstem fMRI data.

claim: Whole-brain analysis of the main effect of temperature showed activation in pain-associated regions such as primary somatosensory cortex, dorsal posterior insula, operculum, anterior cingulate cortex, and cerebellum with larger clusters contralateral to the side of stimulation.
source: Whole-brain analysis of the main effect of temperature (mixed effects analysis, cluster forming threshold Z > 3.1, family wise error (FWE) corrected p < 0.05) showed activation in pain-associated regions such as primary somatosensory cortex, dorsal posterior insula, operculum, anterior cingulate cortex, and cerebellum with larger clusters contralateral to the side of stimulation (i.e. right side of brain).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the whole-brain fMRI data.

claim: A cluster in the medial pre-frontal cortex exhibited deactivation in the main effect of temperature.
source: A cluster in the medial pre-frontal cortex exhibited deactivation.
evidence: This is a finding from the whole-brain fMRI data.

claim: For the main effect of task, bilateral activation was seen in attention and visual processing areas including lateral occipital cortex, anterior insular cortex, and anterior cingulate cortex.
source: For the main effect of task, bilateral activation was seen in attention and visual processing areas including lateral occipital cortex, anterior insular cortex, and anterior cingulate cortex.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the whole-brain fMRI data.

claim: Deactivation was observed in the cerebellum (Crus I), precuneus and lateral occipital cortex (superior division) in the main effect of task.
source: Deactivation was observed in the cerebellum (Crus I), precuneus and lateral occipital cortex (superior division).
evidence: This is a finding from the whole-brain fMRI data.

claim: No cluster in the whole brain analysis reached significance in the positive task*temperature interaction.
source: No cluster in the whole brain analysis reached significance in the positive task*temperature interaction.
evidence: This is a negative finding from the whole-brain fMRI data.

claim: The distribution of patterns of regional brain and brainstem activity were closely similar to those found in previous studies of attentional analgesia.
source: The distribution of these patterns of regional brain and brainstem activity were closely similar to those found in our previous studies of attentional analgesia (Brooks et al., 2017; Oliva et al., 2021a; Oliva et al., 2021b), with the difference that no area in the brain or brainstem showed a task*temperature interaction (unlike the spinal cord).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work.

claim: No area in the brain or brainstem showed a task*temperature interaction (unlike the spinal cord).
source: The distribution of these patterns of regional brain and brainstem activity were closely similar to those found in our previous studies of attentional analgesia (Brooks et al., 2017; Oliva et al., 2021a; Oliva et al., 2021b), with the difference that no area in the brain or brainstem showed a task*temperature interaction (unlike the spinal cord).
evidence: This is a key finding distinguishing brain/brainstem from spinal cord.

claim: The gPPI identified significant modulation of connectivity between ACC and PAG in the main effect of task.
source: The gPPI identified the following pairs of connections [seed-target] as being significantly modulated by our experimental conditions (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2):
evidence: This is a finding from the connectivity analysis.

claim: The gPPI identified significant modulation of connectivity between PAG and RVM in the task*temperature interaction.
source: Permutation testing revealed a significant change in connectivity in the main effect of task contrast between ACC and PAG, and in the task*temperature interaction contrast between PAG and RVM, LC and RVM, and importantly RVM and spinal cord.
evidence: This is a finding from the connectivity analysis.

claim: The gPPI identified significant modulation of connectivity between LC and RVM in the task*temperature interaction.
source: Permutation testing revealed a significant change in connectivity in the main effect of task contrast between ACC and PAG, and in the task*temperature interaction contrast between PAG and RVM, LC and RVM, and importantly RVM and spinal cord.
evidence: This is a finding from the connectivity analysis.

claim: The gPPI identified significant modulation of connectivity between RVM and spinal cord in the task*temperature interaction.
source: Permutation testing revealed a significant change in connectivity in the main effect of task contrast between ACC and PAG, and in the task*temperature interaction contrast between PAG and RVM, LC and RVM, and importantly RVM and spinal cord.
evidence: This is a finding from the connectivity analysis.

claim: The PAG-ACC, RVM-PAG, RVM-rLC, and RVM-Spinal cord connections were stronger in the hard|high versus the easy|high condition.
source: Parameter estimates extracted from the connections modulated by task, revealed that the PAG-ACC, RVM-PAG, RVM-rLC, and RVM-Spinal cord connections were stronger in the hard|high versus the easy|high condition (Figure 4B), consistent with their potential roles in attentional analgesia.
evidence: This is a finding from the connectivity analysis.

claim: The stronger connectivity in hard|high versus easy|high condition is consistent with the potential roles of these connections in attentional analgesia.
source: Parameter estimates extracted from the connections modulated by task, revealed that the PAG-ACC, RVM-PAG, RVM-rLC, and RVM-Spinal cord connections were stronger in the hard|high versus the easy|high condition (Figure 4B), consistent with their potential roles in attentional analgesia.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the connectivity findings.

claim: Neither naltrexone nor reboxetine altered the activations seen for the main effect of temperature at the whole brain level.
source: At the whole brain level, neither drug altered the activations seen for the main effect of temperature.
evidence: This is a finding from the drug comparison analysis.

claim: Only the left anterior insula responded more strongly in the presence of Naltrexone for the main effect of task.
source: Only the left anterior insula responded more strongly in the presence of Naltrexone for the main effect of task (Figure 3—figure supplement 2); however, this was not considered relevant to the analgesic effect as our behavioural findings showed no effect of naltrexone on task performance (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the drug comparison analysis.

claim: A stronger response to temperature was detected in the lower medulla in the presence of naltrexone compared to placebo.
source: In the brainstem, a stronger response to temperature was detected in the lower medulla in the presence of naltrexone compared to placebo (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the drug comparison analysis.

claim: There was no difference between naltrexone and placebo in the main effect of task in the brainstem.
source: There was no difference between naltrexone and placebo in the main effect of task in the brainstem.
evidence: This is a negative finding from the drug comparison analysis.

claim: No differences in either main effect were uncovered in the brainstem for the reboxetine versus placebo comparison.
source: Similarly, no differences in either main effect were uncovered in the brainstem for the reboxetine versus placebo comparison.
evidence: This is a negative finding from the drug comparison analysis.

claim: The administration of naltrexone significantly reduced the connection strength of RVM-spinal cord in the task*temperature interaction.
source: The administration of naltrexone, which abolished attentional analgesia behaviourally, significantly reduced the connection strength of RVM-spinal cord in the task*temperature interaction (Figure 5), indicating a role for opioids in this network interaction.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the drug comparison connectivity analysis.

claim: The reduced RVM-spinal cord connectivity by naltrexone indicates a role for opioids in this network interaction.
source: The administration of naltrexone, which abolished attentional analgesia behaviourally, significantly reduced the connection strength of RVM-spinal cord in the task*temperature interaction (Figure 5), indicating a role for opioids in this network interaction.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the connectivity findings.

claim: The communication between ACC and PAG was significantly weakened by both naltrexone and reboxetine.
source: The communication between ACC and PAG was also significantly weakened by both naltrexone and reboxetine, suggesting this connection to be modulated by both endogenous opioids and noradrenaline (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the drug comparison connectivity analysis.

claim: The ACC-PAG connection is modulated by both endogenous opioids and noradrenaline.
source: The communication between ACC and PAG was also significantly weakened by both naltrexone and reboxetine, suggesting this connection to be modulated by both endogenous opioids and noradrenaline (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the connectivity findings.

claim: The strength of the RVM-LC connection in the main effect of temperature was significantly diminished by reboxetine.
source: The strength of the RVM-LC connection in the main effect of temperature was significantly diminished by reboxetine.
evidence: This is a finding from the drug comparison connectivity analysis.

claim: None of the other connections in the network were altered significantly by the drugs compared to placebo.
source: None of the other connections in the network were altered significantly by the drugs compared to placebo.
evidence: This is a negative finding from the drug comparison connectivity analysis.

claim: The use of individually titrated noxious and innocuous stimuli allowed the identification of a somatotopic Spinalnoci cluster in the main effect of temperature contrast in the dorsal horn of the C6 segment.
source: The use of individually titrated noxious and innocuous stimuli from a thermode applied to the C6 dermatome of the medial forearm, allowed the identification of a somatotopic Spinalnoci cluster in the main effect of temperature contrast in the dorsal horn of the C6 segment.
evidence: This is a methodological statement and finding.

claim: The Spinalnoci cluster pattern was strikingly similar to the pattern of activation noted in several previous focussed spinal imaging pain studies in humans and non-human primates.
source: This was strikingly similar to the pattern of activation noted in several previous focussed spinal imaging pain studies in humans (Brooks et al., 2012; Eippert et al., 2009b; Sprenger et al., 2012; Sprenger et al., 2015; Tinnermann et al., 2017) and non-human primates (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work.

claim: The extracted absolute BOLD from the Spinalnoci cluster was tightly correlated to the pain scores across the four experimental conditions.
source: The extracted absolute BOLD from the Spinalnoci cluster was tightly correlated to the pain scores across the four experimental conditions and therefore the pattern of changes paralleled the changes in pain percept as it was modulated by task.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The pattern of BOLD changes in the Spinalnoci cluster paralleled the changes in pain percept as it was modulated by task.
source: The extracted absolute BOLD from the Spinalnoci cluster was tightly correlated to the pain scores across the four experimental conditions and therefore the pattern of changes paralleled the changes in pain percept as it was modulated by task.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Electrophysiological recordings in non-human primates showed thermal stimulus evoked neural activity in the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve to be altered by attentional focus.
source: This is similar to the seminal findings from electrophysiological recordings in non-human primates (Bushnell et al., 1984), which showed thermal stimulus evoked neural activity in the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve to be altered by attentional focus.
evidence: This is a citation to prior work.

claim: Task related modulation of pain could occur at the first relay point in the nociceptive transmission pathway.
source: Further, it suggested that task related modulation of pain (Miron et al., 1989) could occur at the first relay point in the nociceptive transmission pathway.
evidence: This is an inference from prior work.

claim: Human spinal fMRI by Sprenger et al., 2012 extended the finding of cognitive modulation of nociceptive input and provided evidence that the modulation of pain percept may involve opioids.
source: This finding of cognitive modulation of nociceptive input was extended through human spinal fMRI by Sprenger et al., 2012, who in a second psychophysical experiment with naloxone provided evidence that the modulation of pain percept may involve opioids.
evidence: This is a citation to prior work.

claim: Naltrexone attenuates spinal responses to attentional analgesia, which underlie the behavioural differences between the high|hard and easy|hard conditions.
source: We show that naltrexone attenuates spinal responses to attentional analgesia, which underly the behavioural differences between the high|hard and easy|hard conditions.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study.

claim: The 2 × 2 factorial study design enabled the identification of neural activity reading out the interaction between task and temperature which was only seen at a spinal level in a cluster located deep and medial to the Spinalnoci cluster.
source: Uniquely, our 2 × 2 factorial study design enabled the identification of neural activity reading out the interaction between task and temperature which strikingly was only seen at a spinal level in a cluster located deep and medial to the Spinalnoci cluster.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study.

claim: The activity in the Spinalint cluster was highest in the high|hard condition (ie when the attentional analgesic effect is seen).
source: The activity in this Spinalint cluster was highest in the high|hard condition (ie when the attentional analgesic effect is seen) and this activation was no longer significant in the presence of naltrexone.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The activation in the Spinalint cluster was no longer significant in the presence of naltrexone.
source: The activity in this Spinalint cluster was highest in the high|hard condition (ie when the attentional analgesic effect is seen) and this activation was no longer significant in the presence of naltrexone.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The Spinalint cluster may be consistent with the presence of a local interneuron population in the deeper dorsal horn that could influence the onward transmission of nociceptive information.
source: This may be consistent with the presence of a local interneuron population in the deeper dorsal horn that could influence the onward transmission of nociceptive information (Hughes and Todd, 2020; Koch et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: Such a circuit organisation is predicted by many animal models of pain regulation with the involvement of inhibitory interneurons that shape the incoming signals from the original gate theory through to descending control.
source: Such a circuit organisation is predicted by many animal models of pain regulation with the involvement of inhibitory interneurons that shape the incoming signals from the original gate theory of Melzack and Wall, 1965 through to descending control (Millan, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Opioids like enkephalin are released from local spinal inter-neuronal circuits.
source: For example, opioids like enkephalin are released from such local spinal inter-neuronal circuits (Corder et al., 2018; François et al., 2017) and similarly descending noradrenergic projections exert their influence in part via inhibitory interneurons and an alpha1-adrenoceptor mechanism (Baba et al., 2000a; Baba et al., 2000b; Gassner et al., 2009; Yoshimura and Furue, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Descending noradrenergic projections exert their influence in part via inhibitory interneurons and an alpha1-adrenoceptor mechanism.
source: For example, opioids like enkephalin are released from such local spinal inter-neuronal circuits (Corder et al., 2018; François et al., 2017) and similarly descending noradrenergic projections exert their influence in part via inhibitory interneurons and an alpha1-adrenoceptor mechanism (Baba et al., 2000a; Baba et al., 2000b; Gassner et al., 2009; Yoshimura and Furue, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The ability to resolve the Spinalint cluster may open a window into how local interneuron pools are recruited to shape nociceptive transmission in humans according to cognitive context.
source: As such the ability to resolve this Spinalint cluster may open a window into how such local interneuron pools are recruited to shape nociceptive transmission in humans according to cognitive context.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the implications of the findings.

claim: The study opted to use a single acquisition with identical imaging parameters for the entire CNS.
source: Since our goal was to explore the functional connections between brain, brainstem, and spinal cord, we opted to use a single acquisition, with identical imaging parameters (e.g. orientation of slices, voxel dimensions, point spread function) for the entire CNS.
evidence: This is a methodological choice.

claim: The choice of single acquisition differs from other approaches using different parameters for spinal and brain acquisitions in two fields of view.
source: This differs from other approaches using different parameters for spinal and brain acquisitions in two fields of view (Finsterbusch et al., 2012; Finsterbusch et al., 2013; Islam et al., 2019; Sprenger et al., 2015; Tinnermann et al., 2017 and reviewed in Tinnermann et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a comparison to other methodological approaches.

claim: The choice of single acquisition was motivated by the need to capture signal across the entire CNS region involved in the task and that the use of different acquisition parameters could be a confounding factor for connectivity analyses.
source: Our choice was motivated by (i) the need to capture signal across the entire CNS region involved in the task (including the entire medulla), and (ii) that the use of different acquisition parameters for brain and spinal cord could be a confounding factor, particularly for connectivity analyses, due to altered BOLD sensitivity and point-spread function for the separate image acquisitions.
evidence: This is a justification for the methodological choice.

claim: By taking advantage of the z-shimming approach and the Spinal Cord Toolbox, the study was able to detect significant BOLD signal changes in response to experimental manipulations across the entire CNS.
source: By taking advantage the z-shimming approach (Finsterbusch et al., 2012) and of the recently developed Spinal Cord Toolbox (De Leener et al., 2017), we have been able to detect significant BOLD signal changes in response to experimental manipulations, across the entire CNS.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological success.

claim: Analysis of regional BOLD signal showed activity in both the main effect of task and of temperature in all three of the key brainstem sites PAG, RVM, and LC with no interaction between task and temperature in the brainstem.
source: Analysis of regional BOLD signal showed activity in both the main effect of task and of temperature in all three of the key brainstem sites PAG, RVM, and LC with no interaction between task and temperature in the brainstem providing little indication as to which area might be mediating any analgesic effect (in line with previous Oliva et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: An interaction effect was observed on the effective connectivity between RVM and dorsal horn, with coupling highest in the high|hard conditions.
source: However, an interaction effect was observed on the effective connectivity between RVM and dorsal horn, with coupling highest in the high|hard conditions.
evidence: This is a finding from the connectivity analysis.

claim: The importance of the RVM-spinal cord descending connection to the attentional analgesic effect is emphasised by the effect of naltrexone which blocked both the modulation of RVM-spinal cord connectivity and attentional analgesia.
source: The importance of this descending connection to the attentional analgesic effect is emphasised by the effect of naltrexone which blocked both the modulation of RVM-spinal cord connectivity and attentional analgesia a behavioural finding previously noted by Sprenger et al., 2012.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The findings fit with the classic model of descending pain modulation that has been developed through decades of animal research.
source: This fits with the classic model of descending pain modulation that has been developed through decades of animal research (Fields, 2004; Ossipov et al., 2010) that is engaged in situations of fight or flight and also during appetitive behaviours like feeding and reproduction.
evidence: This is a comparison to established models.

claim: The opioidergic system is engaged moment by moment, in specific contexts, during a relatively simple cognitive task.
source: Here, we identify that the opioidergic system is also engaged moment by moment, in specific contexts, during a relatively simple cognitive tasks and uncover one of its loci of action in humans.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: Analysis of effective connectivity showed evidence for modulation of pathways from ACC to PAG and PAG to RVM by task and the interaction between task and temperature, respectively.
source: Analysis of effective connectivity also showed evidence for modulation of pathways from ACC to PAG and PAG to RVM by task and the interaction between task and temperature, respectively (in agreement with Oliva et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is a finding from the connectivity analysis.

claim: The communication between ACC and PAG was disrupted by the opioid antagonist naltrexone.
source: The communication between ACC and PAG was also disrupted by the opioid antagonist naltrexone.
evidence: This is a finding from the drug comparison connectivity analysis.

claim: Naloxone was shown to disrupt ACC-PAG communication which was linked to the mediation of placebo analgesic effects.
source: This is similar to the previous finding from studies of placebo analgesia where naloxone was shown to disrupt ACC-PAG communication which was also linked to the mediation of its analgesic effects (Eippert et al., 2009a), although behavioural findings of additive analgesia from concurrent placebo and attentional analgesia Buhle et al., 2012 have been used to argue for distinct pathways of mediation.
evidence: This is a citation to prior work.

claim: Activation of the analogous ACC-PAG pathway in rats produces an analgesic effect mediated via an inhibition of activity at a spinal level.
source: Activation of the analogous ACC-PAG pathway in rats has recently been shown to produce an analgesic effect mediated via an inhibition of activity at a spinal level indicating that it indeed represents a component of the descending analgesic system (Drake et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a citation to prior work.

claim: The ACC-PAG pathway in rats failed in a chronic neuropathic pain model.
source: Interestingly, this study also found that this system failed in a chronic neuropathic pain model.
evidence: This is a citation to prior work.

claim: The findings provide evidence for top-down control of spinal nociception during distraction from pain, via the ACC-PAG-RVM-dorsal horn pathway.
source: This provides evidence for top-down control of spinal nociception during distraction from pain, via the ACC-PAG-RVM-dorsal horn pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: The ACC primarily signals the high cognitive load associated with the task to the PAG, that recruits spinally-projecting cells in the RVM.
source: These findings suggest that the ACC primarily signals the high cognitive load associated with the task to the PAG, that recruits spinally-projecting cells in the RVM.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Analgesia could be achieved through disinhibition of spinally-projecting OFF-cells.
source: Analgesia could be achieved through disinhibition of spinally-projecting OFF-cells (Heinricher et al., 1994; Lau and Vaughan, 2014; Roychowdhury and Fields, 1996), that inhibit dorsal horn neurons both directly via GABAergic and opioidergic projections to the primary afferents (Morgan et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2015) and also indirectly via local inhibitory interneuron pools at a spinal level (François et al., 2017) reflected in reduced BOLD signal in the Spinalnoci cluster and activation of the Spinalint pool.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism supported by citations.

claim: Previous human imaging studies have provided evidence for a role of the locus coeruleus in attentional analgesia.
source: Previous human imaging studies have provided evidence for a role of the locus coeruleus in attentional analgesia (Brooks et al., 2017; Oliva et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is a citation to prior work.

claim: The study replicated findings showing activity in the LC related to both task and thermal stimulus as well as interactions between the LC and RVM that were modulated by the interaction between task and temperature.
source: We replicate some of those findings in showing activity in the LC related to both task and thermal stimulus as well as interactions between the LC and RVM that were modulated by the interaction between task and temperature.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The study did not find evidence for an interaction between task and temperature in the LC.
source: However, we neither found evidence for an interaction between task and temperature nor for a correlation with analgesic effect in the LC that we reported in our previous studies (Brooks et al., 2017; Oliva et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is a negative finding from the data analysis.

claim: The study could not demonstrate altered connectivity between the LC and the spinal cord during the paradigm.
source: We also could not demonstrate altered connectivity between the LC and the spinal cord during the paradigm as we anticipated given its known role in descending pain modulation (Hickey et al., 2014; Hirschberg et al., 2017; Llorca-Torralba et al., 2016; Millan, 2002; Oliva et al., 2021b; Ossipov et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a negative finding from the connectivity analysis.

claim: It is likely that the brainstem focussed slice prescription used previously is necessary for capturing sufficient signal from the LC.
source: It is likely that the brainstem focussed slice prescription used previously is necessary for capturing sufficient signal from the LC, and that extending slice coverage to allow inclusion of the spinal cord compromised signal fidelity in this small brainstem nucleus.
evidence: This is a speculation about methodological limitations.

claim: Reboxetine showed a significant analgesic effect which was independent of task difficulty.
source: The noradrenergic manipulation with reboxetine did show a significant analgesic effect which was independent of task difficulty.
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: The dose of reboxetine is capable of altering baseline gain in the nociceptive system, but has no selective effect on attentional pain modulation.
source: This indicates that this dose of reboxetine is capable of altering baseline gain in the nociceptive system, but has no selective effect on attentional pain modulation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral findings.

claim: A post hoc Bayesian paired t-test analysis contrasting reboxetine with placebo showed moderate level of confidence in the null effect on attentional analgesia (Bayes Factor 6.8).
source: We performed a post hoc Bayesian paired t-test analysis contrasting reboxetine with placebo which showed moderate level of confidence in this null effect on attentional analgesia (Bayes Factor 6.8).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post hoc analysis.

claim: Reboxetine modulated a task-dependent connection between ACC and PAG.
source: Reboxetine also modulated a task-dependent connection between ACC and PAG, although this did not appear to influence task performance and so its behavioural significance is uncertain.
evidence: This is a finding from the connectivity analysis.

claim: One potential explanation for the reboxetine findings is that noradrenaline is not involved in attentional analgesia.
source: In interpreting these findings, one potential explanation is that noradrenaline is not involved in attentional analgesia; however, it could also be because of a ceiling effect where the reuptake inhibitor cannot increase the noradrenaline level any further during the attentional task.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Another potential explanation for the reboxetine findings is a ceiling effect where the reuptake inhibitor cannot increase the noradrenaline level any further during the attentional task.
source: In interpreting these findings, one potential explanation is that noradrenaline is not involved in attentional analgesia; however, it could also be because of a ceiling effect where the reuptake inhibitor cannot increase the noradrenaline level any further during the attentional task.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: A noradrenergic antagonist experiment would be ideal to examine the role of noradrenaline in attentional analgesia.
source: In this sense, a noradrenergic antagonist experiment, similar to that used to examine the role of the opioids, would be ideal.
evidence: This is a statement about ideal experimental design.

claim: Selective alpha2-antagonists are not used clinically and experimental agents like Yohimbine have issues that would have confounded the study.
source: However, selective alpha2-antagonists are not used clinically and even experimental agents like Yohimbine have a number of issues that would have confounded this study in that they cause anxiety, excitation and hypertension.
evidence: This is a statement about pharmacological limitations.

claim: The study was not able to provide any additional causal evidence to support a role of the LC in attentional analgesia, but this likely reflects a limitation of the approach and lack of good pharmacological tools.
source: Therefore, we conclude that were not able to provide any additional causal evidence to support a role of the LC in attentional analgesia, but this likely reflects a limitation of our approach and lack of good pharmacological tools to resolve the influence of this challenging target.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the limitations of the study.

claim: The combination of simultaneous whole CNS imaging with concurrent thermal stimulation and attentional task in the context of pharmacological manipulation has enabled the identification of long-range network influences on spinal nociceptive processes and their neurochemistry.
source: This combination of simultaneous whole CNS imaging with concurrent thermal stimulation and attentional task in the context of pharmacological manipulation, has enabled the identification of long-range network influences on spinal nociceptive processes and their neurochemistry.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's contribution.

claim: An important aspect of this approach is that it has enabled the linkage between a large body of fundamental pain neuroscience that focussed on primary afferent to spinal communication and brainstem interactions which can be directly integrated to the findings of whole CNS human imaging.
source: An important aspect of this approach is that it has enabled the linkage between a large body of fundamental pain neuroscience that focussed on primary afferent to spinal communication and brainstem interactions (nociception) which can be directly integrated to the findings of whole CNS human imaging.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of the approach.

claim: The approach offers novel opportunities for translational studies to investigate mechanisms and demonstrate drug target engagement.
source: This also offers novel opportunities for translational studies to investigate mechanisms and demonstrate drug target engagement.
evidence: This is a statement about future applications.

claim: The finding that it is the effective connectivity of these networks that is of importance in the mediation of the effect of attention and the influence of the opioid antagonist reflects recent observations from large scale studies relating psychological measures to functional connectivity.
source: The finding that it is the effective connectivity of these networks that is of importance in the mediation of the effect of attention and the influence of the opioid antagonist reflects recent observations from large scale studies relating psychological measures to functional connectivity (e.g. Dubois et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison to other research.

claim: In patient populations, the focus on long range connectivity may help to differentiate between processes leading to augmented nociception and/or altered perception and control.
source: In patient populations, this focus on long range connectivity may help to differentiate between processes leading to augmented nociception and/or altered perception and control (e.g. in fibromyalgia Oliva et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about clinical applications.

claim: The location of the observed interaction between task and temperature indicates that cognitive tasks are integrated to act at the earliest level in the nociceptive transmission pathway introducing the novel concept of spinal psychology.
source: Finally, we note that the location of the observed interaction between task and temperature indicates that cognitive tasks are integrated to act at the earliest level in the nociceptive transmission pathway introducing the novel concept of spinal psychology.
evidence: This is a novel conceptual interpretation of the findings.

claim: The study was approved by the University of Bristol Faculty of Science Human Research Ethics Committee (reference 23111759828).
source: The study was approved by the University of Bristol Faculty of Science Human Research Ethics Committee (reference 23111759828).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: An initial power analysis was done to determine the sample size using the fmripower software.
source: An initial power analysis was done to determine the sample size using the fmripower software (Mumford and Nichols, 2008).
evidence: This is a description of the study design.

claim: The study was designed to have an 80% power to detect an effect size of 0.425 in the PAG with an alpha of 0.05 requiring a cohort of 40 subjects.
source: Using data from our previous study of attentional analgesia (Brooks et al., 2017, main effect of task contrast in the periaqueductal grey matter mask) we designed the study to have an 80% power to detect an effect size of 0.425 (one sample t-test) in the PAG with an alpha of 0.05 requiring a cohort of 40 subjects.
evidence: This is a description of the study design.

claim: Of 57 subjects screened, two were excluded for claustrophobia, three were excluded for regular or recent drug use, and five were excluded due to intolerance of the thermal stimulus.
source: Of 57 subjects screened, two were excluded for claustrophobia, three were excluded for regular or recent drug use (including recreational), and five were excluded due to intolerance of the thermal stimulus.
evidence: This is a description of the study sample.

claim: Six participants withdrew from the study as they were unable to attend for the full three visits.
source: In addition, six participants withdrew from the study as they were unable to attend for the full three visits.
evidence: This is a description of the study sample.

claim: One participant had an adverse reaction (nausea) to a study drug (naltrexone) and dropped out of the study.
source: One participant had an adverse reaction (nausea) to a study drug (naltrexone) and dropped out of the study.
evidence: This is a description of adverse events.

claim: One subject was excluded for being unable to perform the task correctly.
source: One subject was excluded for being unable to perform the task correctly.
evidence: This is a description of the study sample.

claim: The dose of the opioid antagonist Naltrexone (50 mg) was as per the British National Formulary (BNF) where it is licensed to prevent relapse in opioid or alcohol dependency.
source: The dose of the opioid antagonist Naltrexone (50 mg) was as per the British National Formulary (BNF) where it is licensed to prevent relapse in opioid or alcohol dependency.
evidence: This is a description of the drug dosing rationale.

claim: Naltrexone is well absorbed with high oral bioavailability and its levels in the serum peak after 1 hr with a half-life of between 8 and 12 hr.
source: Naltrexone is well absorbed with high oral bioavailability and its levels in the serum peak after 1 hr with a half-life of between 8 and 12 hr (Verebey et al., 1976).
evidence: This is a statement about drug pharmacokinetics.

claim: Reboxetine has high oral bioavailability (~95%), serum levels peak at around 2 hr after oral administration and it has a half-life of 12 hr.
source: It has high oral bioavailability (~95%), serum levels peak at around 2 hr after oral administration and it has a half-life of 12 hr (Fleishaker, 2000).
evidence: This is a statement about drug pharmacokinetics.

claim: Oral naltrexone (50 mg) produces 95% blockade of mu opioid receptor binding in the brain.
source: Oral naltrexone (50 mg) produces 95% blockade of mu opioid receptor binding in the brain (assessed with Carfentanil PET, Weerts et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a citation to prior work.

claim: Naltrexone (50 mg) altered network activity in a pharmaco-fMRI study and was well tolerated.
source: Additionally, naltrexone (50 mg) altered network activity in a pharmaco-fMRI study and was well tolerated (Morris et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a citation to prior work.

claim: Oral reboxetine (4 mg) has been used successfully in human volunteer studies of affective bias with fMRI neuroimaging.
source: Oral reboxetine (4 mg) has been used successfully in human volunteer studies of affective bias with fMRI neuroimaging (Harmer et al., 2003; Miskowiak et al., 2007).
